bullets: How chemists count atoms they can never count one by one, by weighing them instead
slides.heading: The mole: counting atoms by weighing
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we learn how chemists count atoms by weighing, and by the end you will be able to say what a mole is, turn mass into moles, use mole ratios, and spot the trap that one mole of everything weighs the same.

bullets: Explain what a mole means: a counting word for 6.02 × 10²³ particles, just like a dozen means 12
Use n = m / M to turn mass into moles, and use mole ratios from balanced equations
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the trap about moles all weighing the same.

bullets: A single carbon atom is far too small to count or weigh on its own, yet a 12 g lump of carbon can be weighed in seconds
If weighing can count atoms for us, how many atoms are hiding in that 12 g?
slides.heading: Too many atoms to count
slides.notes: Hold up the idea of weighing a lump of carbon and ask: nobody could count its atoms one by one, so how does the scale help? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the mole is the counting word that makes weighing work.

bullets: A mole is a counting word: 1 mole = 6.02 × 10²³ particles, just as 1 dozen = 12
Molar mass M is the mass of one mole, in g/mol: carbon-12 is 12 g/mol, hydrogen is 1 g/mol, oxygen is 16 g/mol
Moles link mass to particles: n = m / M, and mass = moles x molar mass
slides.heading: The mole counts by weighing
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: a mole always counts the same number of particles, but different particles have different masses, so one mole of each substance weighs a different amount.

bullets: Chemists count particles in moles, the same way a baker counts eggs in dozens
One dozen is 12 items; one mole is 6.02 × 10²³ items - far too many to count one by one, so we weigh moles instead
slides.heading: A mole is a counting word
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the dozen eggs, then the mole of particles. A dozen and a mole are both counting words - they just count very different amounts.

bullets: The mass of one mole of carbon-12 is 12 g - that is its molar mass
Weigh 12 g of carbon and you have exactly one mole: n = m / M = 12 g / 12 g/mol = 1 mol - the scale counted the atoms for you
slides.heading: Mass to moles
slides.notes: Follow the carbon onto the balance and watch the reading reach 12 g. Work the formula aloud: moles equals mass divided by molar mass, so 12 divided by 12 gives exactly one mole.

bullets: Balanced equations count moles, not grams: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O
The mole ratio is 2 : 1 : 2 - double the hydrogen and you must double the oxygen, the ratio never changes
slides.heading: Mole ratios
slides.notes: Trace the equation as the molecules react: two moles of hydrogen react with one mole of oxygen to make two moles of water. Then watch the scale-up: 4 mol of hydrogen needs 2 mol of oxygen and makes 4 mol of water.

bullets: The trap claim is: One mole of anything weighs the same.
Mass = moles x molar mass: one mole of hydrogen is 1 g but one mole of oxygen is 16 g - same number of particles, different mass
slides.heading: A common mistake: one mole of everything weighs the same
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: a mole counts particles, it does not fix the mass. Watch one mole of carbon read 12 g and one mole of water read 18 g on the two pans.

bullets: Step 1: for 12 g of carbon, n = m / M = 12 g / 12 g/mol = 1 mol
Step 2: for the reaction 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, the 2 : 1 : 2 ratio means 1 mol of carbon-style counting scales the same way - double one reactant and the others double too
slides.heading: Worked example: mass to moles and ratios
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: first turn mass into moles with n = m / M, then let the mole ratio in the balanced equation tell you the moles of everything else.

bullets: Calculate the moles in 24 g of carbon and the mass of 2 mol of oxygen, showing n = m / M each time
Careful - a classmate claims: One mole of anything weighs the same. Explain to them why that is wrong, using hydrogen and oxygen
slides.heading: Your turn: weigh, do not guess
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call two pairs: listen for the trap - One mole of anything weighs the same. The fix is Mass = moles x molar mass: one mole of hydrogen is 1 g but one mole of oxygen is 16 g.

bullets: On your own: define a mole and calculate the moles in a given mass using n = m / M
Watch out for the trap one last time: One mole of anything weighs the same. Say why moles of different substances have different masses
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Close by reminding the class of the trap - One mole of anything weighs the same. - and the fix: Mass = moles x molar mass: one mole of hydrogen is 1 g but one mole of oxygen is 16 g. Collect the tickets as they leave and check who still thinks every mole weighs the same.
